capabilities.target: Shell inside the agent's container on a shared CI runner
Org GitHub repository: branch push and PR open
.agent/config.yaml: model, autonomy, max_steps, tools, env, network

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body (public repo)

instructions.note: "You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task" grants the agent standing authority to change its own tool list, model, autonomy, env, and network settings, with no bound on what counts as 'need'.
Scope is 'any issue labeled bug, end to end' combined with self-granted ability to add tools, so the agent's effective capability surface is not fixed at deployment time.

Line 5 instructs the agent to ignore instructions embedded in issues or code; line 6 authorizes the agent to decide, on its own judgment, that a task 'needs' new tools. An attacker can phrase a technical requirement rather than an imperative instruction, triggering line 6 without tripping the line 5 defense.

The only defenses against destructive commands, secret exfiltration, and indirect prompt injection are two natural-language instructions. No structural control (egress allowlist, credential scoping, input classifier) backs either rule, against an untrusted-input surface open to any GitHub user.

controls.name: Container isolation on shared CI runner
controls.decay_rationale: Contains host OS escalation from cap.shell, but places no restriction on outbound network or on which credentials the shell process can read, so it does not contain data exfiltration or self-reconfiguration.

controls.name: Prompt instruction forbidding destructive or exfiltrating commands
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model recognizing disguised destructive or exfiltrating commands and refusing them; a more capable model follows longer injected goals and rationalizes exceptions (control_decay.md row 1).

controls.name: Prompt instruction to ignore instructions embedded in issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: Spotlighting-style defense against indirect injection, defeated by adaptive phrasing and by the standing self-config authorization in prompt.md:6, which does not require the model to perceive text as 'an instruction' to act on it.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist
controls.decay_rationale: Would remove the general-internet exfiltration channel. Does not fully close the finding, since GitHub itself remains a legitimate, reachable destination for secrets embedded in commits or PR content.

controls.name: Scope GITHUB_TOKEN to least privilege: single repo, no workflow scope, short-lived
controls.decay_rationale: Does not decay with model capability. Narrows blast radius from all org repos to one, and removes credential_access value from a successful shell compromise.

controls.name: Human approval gate before branch push or PR creation
Make .agent/config.yaml read-only to the agent at runtime; changes only via reviewed PR
controls.decay_rationale: If the file is mounted read-only or editing requires a separate reviewed pipeline, cap.self_config becomes unreachable by the model under any behavior, which severs the self-modification path.

controls.name: Tamper-evident logging of shell commands, config edits, and pushes, attributable to the triggering issue
Structural isolation of issue/code content from command construction, plus an injection classifier
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier sees content, not intent, and is defeated by multi-document or encoded payloads; still raises cost of a successful injection compared to a bare instruction.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted issue content reaches shell execution with a broad org-wide credential and unrestricted egress

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can open an issue and apply the 'bug' label through the issue template.
Agent runs 'whatever commands it needs' to reproduce and test, with ORG_WIDE_PAT (repo+workflow, all org repos) in env and network: unrestricted.
Agent pushes a branch and opens a PR; this is a reachable, attacker-readable egress channel for anything placed in commit content, branch names, or PR text, independent of the raw-network channel.

forecast.watch_signal: subject.model.swappable is true (model: latest); a model id/version change in .agent/config.yaml with no corresponding review.

evidence.observation: ORG_WIDE_PAT with repo+workflow scope on all org repos is readable by any shell command.
Any GitHub user can open issues and add the 'bug' label through an issue template, making the trigger fully untrusted-reachable.
Only behavioral instructions guard against destructive/exfiltrating commands and embedded instructions.

recommendations.action: Deploy a network egress allowlist restricted to required hosts; deny general internet.
Scope GITHUB_TOKEN to the single target repo, remove workflow scope, rotate or issue short-lived tokens per task.
Require a raw-action human approval gate before branch push or PR creation, showing the full diff and destination from the system of record.
Add tamper-evident logging of shell commands and pushes attributable to the triggering issue.

findings.title: Self-modification (TC3): untrusted issue content can induce persistent self-reconfiguration via the agent's standing authority to edit its own config

attack_path.note: Attacker phrases a technical 'requirement' rather than an imperative instruction, so it is not recognized as 'an instruction inside the issue' under prompt.md:5.
prompt.md:6 authorizes the agent to adjust .agent/config.yaml 'if it needs extra tools'; nothing bounds which fields (tools, env, network, autonomy, model) may change, or reviews the change.
The modified configuration governs every subsequent run, persisting the compromise across sessions.

forecast.watch_signal: Diff of .agent/config.yaml tools/env/network/autonomy fields between runs; any unreviewed change.

evidence.observation: "You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task" with no scope limit on what may be changed.
All of these fields live in the file the agent is authorized to edit.

recommendations.action: Make .agent/config.yaml read-only to the agent at runtime; route any tool/config change through a reviewed PR merged by a human.
Remove prompt.md:6 entirely; self-reconfiguration should never be a model-discretion decision.

findings.title: Unbounded autonomous execution on a shared CI runner with no step or runtime limit (ASI08)

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can trigger the agent at will; no rate limit on task initiation is declared.
max_steps: null and no max_runtime_minutes; the agent can run or loop arbitrarily long with a broad credential and unrestricted network on infrastructure shared with other teams.

forecast.watch_signal: Median steps or runtime per task trending upward with no step/runtime limit configured; shared-runner resource or cost alerts.

evidence.observation: max_steps: null, no runtime bound declared anywhere in the artifacts.
Runs in a container on a shared CI runner with outbound internet; any GitHub user can trigger it via the issue template.

recommendations.action: Set max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes; rate-limit task intake per issue author; move to ephemeral, per-task dedicated runners instead of a shared runner.

findings.title: Forecast: planned Slack MCP server would extend the self-config path into an unpinned, unvetted egress channel (ASI04/ASI07)

attack_path.note: Attacker-influenced issue convinces the agent it 'needs' the Slack integration to finish a task.
Agent adds the new MCP server entry to .agent/config.yaml using the authority already granted in prompt.md:6.
New, as yet unspecified external server/tool with no stated identity verification or definition pinning.

forecast.watch_signal: A new MCP server entry (e.g., Slack) appearing in .agent/config.yaml tools, or a new A2A/MCP client config entry, with no server authentication, identity verification, or definition pinning declared.

evidence.observation: "The team wants to add a Slack MCP server next quarter." No detail on auth, identity verification, or definition pinning is yet available.
The self-config authority already in place is the exact mechanism by which this addition would occur without a separate review step.

recommendations.action: Before connecting any new MCP server, require signed or pinned tool definitions, verified peer identity, least-privilege credentials, and treat server output as untrusted input; re-run this assessment under ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.2 before deployment.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: untrusted GitHub issue content (anyone can open one and apply the 'bug' label) reaches shell execution holding an org-wide, repo+workflow-scoped PAT with unrestricted network egress, an irreversible self-configure capability, and a push/PR egress channel, under full (A4) autonomy with no step or runtime limit. Residual risk stays critical because one path (f3: unbounded autonomous execution on a shared CI runner) is covered by no control at all — the two existing prompt instructions address destructive/exfiltrating commands and embedded instructions, not runaway steps or runtime. The other two present findings (f1 exfiltration, f2 self-reconfiguration) drop only to high, credited solely for behavioral, capability-dependent prompt instructions (rubric step 4, -1 tier), since no structural control severs or meaningfully gates either path today. Forecast risk remains critical: a model upgrade (subject.model.swappable is true) removes the only credit those two findings have, returning them to critical, and the planned Slack MCP server addition would extend the self-config path (already unreviewed) into a new, unvetted external channel. The single control whose decay moves the most mass is the pair of behavioral prompt instructions (control.no_delete_no_exfil_instruction, control.ignore_embedded_instructions): they are the only credited controls in the entire design, and both are dependent on model compliance.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; no transcripts, logs, or live traces were reviewed.

No formal MCP/tool manifest or IaC was provided for the CI runner; sandbox strength (whether cap.shell can reach the host OS or other tenants) is inferred from runtime notes alone, so confidence on control.sandbox_container's effectiveness is medium at best.

No detail is available on the planned Slack MCP server beyond a one-line mention; finding f4 is necessarily low confidence and will need reassessment once that integration is designed (ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.2 significant change).

Whether in.repo_files can be influenced by external contributors (e.g., merged PRs from non-maintainers) was not stated; it was conservatively scored as internal trust rather than untrusted, which could understate risk if the repository accepts external contributions.
